old: Elizabeth suspected she was the first person who had ever dared to trifle with such grand impertinence.
new: Elizabeth suspected she was the first person who had ever dared to trifle with so much dignified rudeness.
reason: 'Such grand impertinence' reads as if Elizabeth is the impertinent one; the point is that Lady Catherine's own lofty rudeness has never been teased before.
lead_note: Source 'dignified impertinence'; the rudeness is clearly Lady Catherine's

old: Lady Catherine, Sir William, and Mr. and Mrs. Collins sat down to quadrille. Since Miss de Bourgh chose to play casino,
new: Lady Catherine, Sir William, and Mr. and Mrs. Collins sat down to the card game quadrille. Since Miss de Bourgh chose to play casino, another card game,
reason: Quadrille and casino are period card games; 'play casino' in particular now suggests gambling at a casino.
lead_note: Brief glosses; 'casino' would otherwise suggest a gambling house

old: There were two nephews of Lady Catherine requiring them,
new: There were two nephews of Lady Catherine to whom he owed his respects,
reason: 'Them' refers back to 'his respects' in the previous sentence, which is too far away and too abstract; the clause reads as if the nephews need something.
lead_note: Referent clarified; the source says 'to require them' (his respects)

old: And though there were not many of her acquaintances she did not prefer to him,
new: And though she preferred most of her acquaintances to him,
reason: Stacked negatives ('not many ... she did not prefer') make readers stop to work out that she dislikes him.
lead_note: Stacked negative resolved; the source means she preferred most of them

old: _His_ eyes had been quickly and repeatedly turned toward them with a look of curiosity, and that her Ladyship eventually shared the feeling was more openly shown, for she did not hesitate to call out:
new: _His_ eyes had quickly and repeatedly turned toward them with a look of curiosity, and her Ladyship soon showed the same curiosity more openly, for she did not hesitate to call out:
reason: A 'that'-clause as subject ('that her Ladyship ... shared the feeling was more openly shown') has to be re-read.

old: by coming over in such state to listen
new: by coming over with such ceremony to listen
reason: 'In such state' (meaning with such ceremony or grandeur) is no longer understood and may read as 'in such a state' (agitated).

old: that he might just as easily have married _her_, had she been his relative.
new: that he might just as well have married Miss Bingley, had she been his relative.
reason: The sentence mentions Miss de Bourgh just before, so '_her_' seems to mean Miss de Bourgh; it actually means Miss Bingley. That reverses the joke.
lead_note: Restores the source's order: in the source Miss Bingley is the antecedent of _her_

old: Colonel Fitzwilliam had made it clear that he had no intentions at all,
new: Colonel Fitzwilliam had made it clear that he had no intentions toward her at all,
reason: 'No intentions at all' is too bare now; it means he has no intention of courting or marrying her.
lead_note: 'Intentions' in the period's marriage sense, made clear

old: His sense of her inferiority, of it being beneath him,
new: His sense of her inferiority, of such a match being beneath him,
reason: 'It' has no antecedent (it means the match, or marrying her).

old: But the approaching figure was now close enough to see her, and stepping forward eagerly, called her name.
new: But he was now close enough to see her, and, stepping forward eagerly, he called her name.
reason: The second clause has no subject. As written, 'the approaching figure' does the calling, which is awkward, and the 'and' clause is missing 'he'.

old: who had chances to observe him in unguarded moments that Mr. Darcy never had.
new: who had chances to observe him in unguarded moments that my father never had.
reason: Darcy is the letter-writer, so 'Mr. Darcy' here reads as Darcy referring to himself in the third person. It actually means his father.
lead_note: In the letter Darcy calls his father 'Mr. Darcy'; 'my father' removes the confusion

old: make up for those minor failings she would try to classify Mr. Darcy's description of years of idleness and vice as being.
new: make up for those casual errors—which was how she would try to class what Mr. Darcy had described as years of idleness and vice.
reason: Tangled clause ending in a stranded 'as being'. Readers have to reverse-engineer it.
lead_note: Untangled, and brought closer to the source ('casual errors, under which she would endeavour to class')

old: had long ago confirmed his blamelessness in the affair
new: had long ago confirmed Darcy's blamelessness in the affair
reason: One very long chain of 'that ...' clauses joined by dashes, with 'his' switching between Bingley and Darcy. A listener loses the thread; 'his blamelessness' seems to mean Bingley's.
lead_note: Only the referent is fixed; Austen's long chain of admissions is kept as it is

old: satisfied my vanity with useless or pointless suspicion
new: satisfied my vanity with useless suspicion, or suspicion of the blameless
reason: 'Useless or pointless' is redundant and flat, which weakens the climax of the self-reproach.
lead_note: Fidelity: the source's 'useless or blameless distrust' was flattened to 'useless or pointless'. The fix restores 'blameless'.
